Surah (a chapter of the Qur'an): a predicate of an implied subject, or a subject whose predicate is omitted, the sense being "in what We have sent down to you is a surah." "We sent it down" is a description of the surah. ﴿And We made it obligatory﴾: that is, We made obligatory the rulings contained in it. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read ﴿farradnāhā﴾ with the doubled letter (ra), for emphasis. ﴿Clear verses﴾: meaning the admonitions, rulings and parables it contains. It was also said: the meaning of "clear" here is that nothing in it is ambiguous.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 24, verse 2–3:

﴿The adulterer and the adulteress: flog each one of them with a hundred lashes.﴾ "The adulterer and the adulteress" (al-zaniyah wa'l-zani) is meant as a generic category. The adulteress is mentioned first because adultery was then more common among women, for among them were slave-girls and prostitutes who openly practised it. The grammatical construction of "al-zani wa'l-zaniyah" is like that of "al-sariq wa'l-sariqah" in "cut off their hands," which was mentioned in al-Ma'idah [38]. This verse abrogates, by scholarly consensus (ijma'; scholarly consensus), what is in Surah al-Nisa' [14] regarding confinement in houses, which is in one verse, and harm (adha), which is in the other. Then, according to Malik, the wording of this verse is not general, for the flogging in al-Ma'idah is the prescribed punishment (hadd) only for an adulterer and adulteress who are Muslim, free, and not previously married. Thus, disbelievers are excluded, and they are referred back to the people of their own religion. Slaves, both male and female, and the married (muhsan and muhsanah) are also excluded. As for slaves, male and female, their punishment is fifty lashes, whether they are married or unmarried. As for the free married pair, their punishment is stoning. This is according to the school of Malik.

As for discussing the verse from the standpoint of the other schools, know that the apparent meaning of this verse is general, covering Muslims and disbelievers, free persons, slaves and slave-girls, and both married and unmarried persons. Then the scholars specified some exceptions from this generality, some by consensus and some by disagreement. As for disbelievers, Abu Hanifah and the Zahiris (Ahl al-Zahir; literalist school) held that their punishment is a hundred lashes, whether they were married or not, taking the generality of the verse. Al-Shafi'i held that their punishment is the same as that of Muslims: lashing if unmarried, and stoning if married, relying on the verse and on the Prophet's ﷺ stoning of a Jewish man and woman when they committed adultery. Malik held that they should be referred to the people of their religion, based on the words of God Most High in Surah al-Nisa': ﴿And those of your women who commit lewdness﴾ [al-Nisa': 15], which he took as specific to Muslim women, on the view that this was abrogated by this verse, but its ruling remained in its place. As for slaves, the Zahiris held that the punishment of a slave-girl is fifty lashes, based on the words of God Most High: ﴿Upon them is half the punishment of free married women﴾ [al-Nisa': 25], and that the punishment of a male slave is a hundred lashes, by the generality of the verse. Others said that a male slave is flogged fifty times by analogy to the slave-girl, since there is no difference between them. As for the married person, the majority said that his punishment is stoning, so he is specified from this verse. Some of them call this specification abrogation (naskh). Then they differed regarding the specifier or the abrogator. It was said: it is the verse whose wording was lifted but whose ruling remained, which is His saying: ﴿The married man and the married woman, if they commit adultery, stone them outright as an exemplary punishment from God, and God is Mighty and Wise.﴾ It was also said: its abrogator is the established sunnah concerning stoning. The Zahiris and Ali ibn Abi Talib said: the married person is flogged by this verse and then stoned by the sunnah, so they combined the two punishments on him, and they did not regard this verse as abrogated or specified. The Kharijites said: there is no stoning at all, for stoning is not in the Book of God. Their view is not taken into account. The apparent meaning of the verse is flogging without exile (taghrib). Abu Hanifah also said this. Malik said: flogging and exile are a sunnah, based on the hadith, which is his ﷺ saying: "A virgin with a virgin: a hundred lashes and a year's exile." According to Malik, there is no exile for women or for slaves. The manner of flogging according to Malik is on the back, with the flogged person seated. Al-Shafi'i said: the lashes are distributed over all the limbs, and the flogged person stands. A woman is covered with a garment that does not protect her from the blows. According to Malik, a man is stripped. Some people said he is flogged over a shirt.

﴿And let not pity for them take hold of you﴾: it was said: this means in suspending the punishment, i.e., establish it without fail. It was also said: it means in the lightness of the blows. It was said: it means both. According to the first view, the beating for adultery is like the beating for slander (qadhf), not severe, which is the school of Malik and al-Shafi'i. According to the second and third views, the beating for adultery is harsher. There was disagreement as to whether it is permissible to gather a hundred lashes and strike with them once. Malik forbade it, and Abu Hanifah permitted it, based on what is related in the story of Ayyub, peace be upon him. Al-Shafi'i permitted it for the sick, because this is related in a hadith.

﴿And let a group of the believers witness their punishment﴾: the purpose of this is the rebuke of the adulterers and the severity upon them. There was disagreement about the minimum number that suffices from the group. It was said: four, by analogy with the testimony for adultery, and this is the view of Ibn Abi Zayd. It was said: ten. It was said: two, and this is the well-known position of Malik's school. It was said: one.

﴿The adulterer does not marry except an adulteress or a polytheist﴾: the meaning is condemnation of adulterers and reprehension of adultery, and that it is not committed except by an adulterer or a polytheist, and no woman agrees to it except an adulteress or a polytheist. "Yankihu" (marries) here is in the sense of "yujami'" (has intercourse). It was also said: the meaning is that it is not lawful for an adulterer to marry except an adulteress or a polytheist, and not lawful for an adulteress to marry except an adulterer or a polytheist. Then this ruling was abrogated, and it was permitted for them to marry whomever they wish. The first view is the correct one.

﴿And that has been forbidden to the believers﴾: the reference of "that" is to adultery, i.e., adultery has been forbidden to the believers. It was also said: the reference is to a believer who is not an adulterer marrying an adulteress, for some people forbade him to marry her. This is based on the second view regarding the preceding verse, and it is far-fetched. Malik and others permitted his marrying her, and it is reported from him that he disliked it.

This is the prescribed punishment for slander (qadhf), the false accusation that God expresses by the word "casting" (ramy). The chaste women (al-muhsanat) here means virtuous women. He singled them out because slandering them is more common and more heinous than slandering men, yet men are included in the ruling by implication, since there is no difference between them. The scholars agreed that the ruling for men and women here is the same. It was also said that the meaning is "those who cast accusations at chaste persons (anfus al-muhsanat)," so that the wording on this reading covers both men and women.

Here one must discuss slander, the one slandered, and the testimony relating to it. As for slander, it is the accusation of unlawful sexual intercourse (zina), which is agreed upon. According to Malik and al-Shafi'i it also includes accusing someone of the deed of the people of Lot (sodomy), on the basis of the general wording of "casting" in the verse, but Abu Hanifah disagreed. It also includes denying a person's lineage. The school of Malik holds that an allusive (ta'ridh) accusation of all of these is equivalent to an explicit one, whereas al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifah disagreed.

As for the slanderer, he is punished, whether he is Muslim or disbelieving, because of the general wording of the verse, and whether he is free or a slave. However, according to the majority, a slave or slave-woman is punished with forty lashes only, and their punishment is halved by analogy (qiyas) with the halving of the punishment for unlawful intercourse. This goes against the Zahiris. A boy and a madman are not punished, because they are not legally responsible (mukallaf).

As for the one slandered, the school of Malik stipulates that he must be Muslim, sane, adult, free, and innocent of what he was accused of, and capable of sexual intercourse, to guard against the castrated and the like. Therefore, according to him, one who slanders a boy, a disbeliever, a castrated man, or a slave is not punished, nor one who is incapable of intercourse. It has also been said that one who slanders any of these is punished, on the basis of the general wording of the verse. They agreed on the requirement of innocence from what one was accused of.

As for the testimony that removes the punishment for slander, it is that two upright witnesses testify that the one slandered is a slave or a disbeliever, or that four upright male witnesses testify by direct observation to what he was accused of, like the kohl-stick entering the kohl-pot, and they give their testimony together.

﴿Except those who repent﴾. Before this exception, three rulings were mentioned: the punishment, the rejection of the slanderer's testimony, and his being declared a transgressor (fasiq). They agreed that the exception refers to the designation as a transgressor, and that this is lifted from him by repentance. They agreed that it does not refer to the punishment, and that the punishment is not dropped by repentance. They disagreed over whether it refers to the rejection of testimony. Malik said: if he repents, his testimony is accepted, but Abu Hanifah disagreed. His repentance is the rectification of his condition in his religion and his retraction of his accusation.

This verse concerns a husband accusing his wife, which makes li'an (mutual oaths of cursing, sworn between spouses in accusation) obligatory. Its occasion was that a man said, "O Messenger of Allah, if a man finds another man with his wife, should he kill him, and then you kill him? Or what should he do?" The Prophet ﷺ remained silent. The man came back and repeated the same question, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "Allah has revealed concerning you and your wife. Bring her." So she was brought, and they performed li'an, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ separated them.

According to Malik, the grounds for li'an are two: first, that the husband claims he saw his wife committing adultery; second, that he denies the child she is carrying, claiming that he had made istibra' (ascertaining that she was clear of pregnancy) before it. When the husband performs li'an, three rulings attach to it: the punishment for slander (hadd al-qadhf) is lifted from him; the child is severed from him; and the punishment for adultery becomes obligatory upon her if she does not perform li'an. If she performs li'an, the punishment is dropped from her.

The wording of the verse is general, covering free wives and slave wives, Muslim and non-Muslim women, and upright and other women. Malik adopted this view and made Islam a condition for the husband, whereas Abu Hanifa made it a condition that both spouses be Muslim, free, and upright.

﴿So the testimony of one of them is four testimonies by Allah that he is surely among the truthful﴾: that is, the husband says four times, "I bear witness by Allah that I saw this woman committing adultery," or "I bear witness by Allah that this pregnancy is not from me, and that she has committed adultery, and that in this I am surely among the truthful." Then in the fifth he says, "May the curse of Allah be upon me if I am among the liars." Ashhab added that he should say, "I bear witness by Allah, besides whom there is no god."

The phrase ﴿أَرْبَعُ شَهَادَاتٍ بِٱللَّهِ﴾ is in the accusative as an absolute object (منصوب على المصدرية), and its governing element is the noun شهادة in ﴿شَهَادَةُ أَحَدِهِمْ﴾. It was read in the nominative (بالرفع), as the predicate of شهادة أحدهم. The phrase ﴿بِٱللَّهِ إِنَّهُ لَمِنَ ٱلصَّادِقِينَ﴾ is attached either to ﴿أَرْبَعُ شَهَادَاتٍ﴾ or to ﴿شَهَادَةُ أَحَدِهِمْ﴾.

﴿And the fifth [testimony] is that the curse of Allah be upon him if he is among the liars﴾: here ﴿الْخَامِسَةُ﴾ is read in the accusative (بنصب الخامسة) in this place and in the second place. It is governed by an implied verb, as if to say "and he testifies the fifth," or it is coordinated with ﴿أَرْبَعَ شَهَادَاتٍ﴾ in the accusative reading. The rest of the readers read it in the nominative (بالرفع), either as the subject of a nominal sentence (على الابتداء) or as coordinated with ﴿شَهَادَةُ أَحَدِهِمْ﴾ in the nominative reading.

It was also read as أن لعنه and أن غضب, with the particle أن doubled (بتشديد أن) and its noun in the accusative. Nafi' read it with the particle lightened (بتخفيفها) and the nouns ﴿اللَّعْنَةَ﴾ and ﴿الْغَضَبَ﴾ in the nominative, as subjects of nominal sentences (على الابتداء).

﴿And it shall avert from her the punishment that she testify four testimonies by Allah that he is surely among the liars﴾: the punishment here is the punishment for adultery. Her li'an averts it. Her li'an consists of her saying four times, "I bear witness by Allah that I did not commit adultery," and that he is surely among the liars in this. Then in the fifth she says, "May the wrath of Allah be upon me if he is among the truthful." Three rulings attach to her li'an: the punishment is averted from her; she is separated from her husband; and the prohibition (al-hurmah) becomes permanent.

﴿So the testimony of one of them is four testimonies by Allah that he is surely among the truthful﴾: that is, the husband says four times, "I bear witness by Allah that I saw this woman committing adultery," or "I bear witness by Allah that this pregnancy is not from me, and that she has committed adultery, and that in this I am surely among the truthful." Then in the fifth he says, "May the curse of Allah be upon me if I am among the liars." Ashhab added that he should say, "I bear witness by Allah, besides whom there is no god."

The phrase ﴿أَرْبَعُ شَهَادَاتٍ بِٱللَّهِ﴾ is in the accusative as an absolute object (منصوب على المصدرية), and its governing element is the noun شهادة in ﴿شَهَادَةُ أَحَدِهِمْ﴾. It was read in the nominative (بالرفع), as the predicate of شهادة أحدهم. The phrase ﴿بِٱللَّهِ إِنَّهُ لَمِنَ ٱلصَّادِقِينَ﴾ is attached either to ﴿أَرْبَعُ شَهَادَاتٍ﴾ or to ﴿شَهَادَةُ أَحَدِهِمْ﴾.

﴿And the fifth [testimony] is that the curse of Allah be upon him if he is among the liars﴾: here ﴿الْخَامِسَةُ﴾ is read in the accusative (بنصب الخامسة) in this place and in the second place. It is governed by an implied verb, as if to say "and he testifies the fifth," or it is coordinated with ﴿أَرْبَعَ شَهَادَاتٍ﴾ in the accusative reading. The rest of the readers read it in the nominative (بالرفع), either as the subject of a nominal sentence (على الابتداء) or as coordinated with ﴿شَهَادَةُ أَحَدِهِمْ﴾ in the nominative reading.

It was also read as أن لعنه and أن غضب, with the particle أن doubled (بتشديد أن) and its noun in the accusative. Nafi' read it with the particle lightened (بتخفيفها) and the nouns ﴿اللَّعْنَةَ﴾ and ﴿الْغَضَبَ﴾ in the nominative, as subjects of nominal sentences (على الابتداء).

﴿And it shall avert from her the punishment that she testify four testimonies by Allah that he is surely among the liars﴾: the punishment here is the punishment for adultery. Her li'an averts it. Her li'an consists of her saying four times, "I bear witness by Allah that I did not commit adultery," and that he is surely among the liars in this. Then in the fifth she says, "May the wrath of Allah be upon me if he is among the truthful." Three rulings attach to her li'an: the punishment is averted from her; she is separated from her husband; and the prohibition (al-hurmah) becomes permanent.

﴿And were it not for the bounty of Allah﴾ — the response (jawab) of the conditional particle لو (law, "if") is omitted here, and likewise in the other passage. Its implied form is ﴿And were it not for the bounty of Allah upon you﴾ [and His mercy…], ﴿He would have seized you﴾ (لآخذكم), or something similar to this.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 24, verse 11:

﴿Indeed, those who brought the slander are a group among you.﴾ Al-ifk (slander): the most severe lying. This verse and what follows, up to the completion of sixteen verses, were revealed concerning our mistress 'Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her) and her innocence of what the people of slander accused her of. Allah cleared four people with four things: He cleared Yusuf (Joseph) through the testimony of a witness from her own family; He cleared Musa (Moses) of the claim of the Jews through the stone that ran off with his garment; He cleared Maryam (Mary) through the speech of her child in her lap; and He cleared 'Aisha of the slander through the revelation of the Qur'an concerning her. These verses contain the utmost degree of care for her, honour for her, and severe warning against whoever slanders her.

The hadith of the slander was related by al-Bukhari, Muslim and others. Its summary is that 'Aisha went out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the expedition of Banu al-Mustaliq. Her necklace was lost, so she lagged behind searching for it until the people set off. A man called Safwan ibn al-Mu'attal came, saw her, dismounted from his camel and stepped aside until 'Aisha had mounted. He then led the camel until he reached the army. The people of slander said what they said about that. When this reached the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "What is the matter with men who have slandered my family? By Allah, I know nothing of my family except good. And they have mentioned a man of whom I know nothing except good." He also asked the servant-girl of 'Aisha, and she said: "By Allah, I know nothing of her except what the goldsmith knows of red pure gold."

Al-'usbah (the group) is a company of ten to forty. Only four are mentioned in the hadith as being from the people of slander: 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, the leader of the hypocrites; Hamnah bint Jahsh; Mistah ibn Uthathah; and Hassan ibn Thabit. It is also said that Hassan was not among them. ('Usbah) is in the nominative because it is the predicate of inna (the predicate of inna, the particle of emphasis). Ibn 'Atiyyah chose that 'usbah be a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in jaa'u (they came), with the predicate being ﴿Do not think it bad for you﴾, on the assumption that the matter is: "Indeed, the story of those who brought the slander..." However, the first view is more apparent.

﴿Rather, it is good for you﴾ is addressed to the Muslims. The good in this lies in five aspects: the clearing of the Mother of the Believers; Allah's honour for her by revealing revelation concerning her; the great reward for her from the slander against her; a lesson for the believers; and the retribution against the slanderers.

﴿And the one who took upon himself the greater part of it﴾ is 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, the hypocrite. It is also said that the one who initiated this slander was not specified. The great punishment here may refer either to the prescribed punishment (hadd) or to the punishment of the Hereafter.

"Why did you not, when you heard it, think well of one another, the believing men and believing women, and say, 'This is an obvious lie'?" — no, I must translate only the given passage, as instructed.

Here is the translation:

﴿Why, when you heard it, did the believing men and believing women not think well of their own selves?﴾ Here "lawla" (why not / would that) is used for reproach (ʿaraḍ), and the meaning is: it was incumbent upon the believing men and believing women to measure that matter against themselves. If such a thing would be far-fetched in their own case, then it is even further-fetched in the case of ʿĀ'isha, because of her excellence. It is narrated that this reflection occurred to Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, and he said to his wife, "Would you have done such a thing?" She said, "No, by Allah." He said, "Then is ʿĀ'isha better than you?" She said, "Yes." If it is asked: why did He say "sami'tumūhu" (you heard it) in the second-person address, then shift to the third-person form in His words "ẓanna al-mu'minūna" (the believing men thought), and not say "ẓanntum" (you thought)? The answer is that this is an iltifat (shift of grammatical person), intended for emphasis and for explicitly stating faith, which requires that a believer not attribute evil to another believer.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 24, verse 13–14:

﴿Why did they not bring four witnesses against her?﴾ Here, *lawla* (لولا) is used to express reproach (ʿarḍ). The pronoun in ﴿they did not bring﴾ refers to the people of the slander (ahl al-ifk). Then God judged them to be liars, since they did not bring the witnesses. ﴿You plunged into it﴾: it is said that *afāḍa fīhi* and *khāḍa fīhi* (to plunge into it) mean to speak about it at great length when one talks a great deal about it.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 24, verse 13–14:

﴿Why did they not bring four witnesses against her?﴾ Here, *lawla* (لولا) is used to express reproach (ʿarḍ). The pronoun in ﴿they did not bring﴾ refers to the people of the slander (ahl al-ifk). Then God judged them to be liars, since they did not bring the witnesses. ﴿You plunged into it﴾: it is said that *afāḍa fīhi* and *khāḍa fīhi* (to plunge into it) mean to speak about it at great length when one talks a great deal about it.

Qur'anic quotations: ﴿إِذْ تَلَقَّوْنَهُ بِأَلْسِنَتِكُمْ﴾ = "When you received it with your tongues."

Translation of the commentary:

"When you received it with your tongues" (﴿إِذْ تَلَقَّوْنَهُ بِأَلْسِنَتِكُمْ﴾). The word إذ (idh, "when") is governed (al-'amil, the governing element) by either the phrase ﴿لَمَسَّكُمْ﴾ (lamassakum, "would have touched you") or ﴿أَفَضْتُمْ﴾ (afadtum, "you plunged into"). The meaning of ﴿تَلَقَّوْنَهُ﴾ (talaqqawnahu, "you received it") is that some of you take it from others. In this statement, and in what comes before and after it, there is a rebuke to them for their engagement in discussing the tale of the slander (hadith al-ifk), even though they had not believed it. The obligation was to turn away from mentioning it and to abandon it entirely. So He rebuked them for three things: their receiving it with their tongues, that is, asking about it and taking it from the one who was asked; second, their saying that; and third, that they considered it a trivial matter while it was grave in the sight of God. The benefit of His saying ﴿بِأَلْسِنَتِكُمْ﴾ (bi-alsinatikum, "with your tongues") and "with your mouths" is to indicate that this talk was by the tongue and not by the heart, since they did not know its reality in their hearts.

﴿And why, when you heard it, did you not say, "It is not for us to speak of this"?﴾ That is, it was obligatory for them to hasten to deny this report as soon as they first heard it. Also, in this verse there is an interposition (ʿaraḍ, a parenthetical insertion) with the word "lawlā." Its proper placement was that the verb should follow it directly, without any separation between them, as in His words ﴿when you heard it﴾. This is because adverbial expressions (ẓurūf) permit what is not permitted in other constructions. The purpose of placing this adverbial expression first is to give it importance, and to show that it was obligatory to hasten to deny the speech at the first moment you heard it. The meaning of ﴿it is not for us﴾ is: it is not fitting for us, nor lawful for us, to speak of this.

﴿Glory be to You﴾ is a declaration of God's transcendence above being the wife of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), as the people of the slander (ahl al-ifk) claimed. Al-Zamakhsharī said: it carries the sense of wonder at the enormity of the matter and of deeming it far-fetched. The basis for this is that God is glorified when witnessing wondrous things. ﴿This is a tremendous slander (buhtān ʿaẓīm)﴾. Slander (buhtān) is saying about a person what is not in him, while backbiting (ghība), which is a related concept, is saying what is in him.

Qur'anic quotations in ﴿ ﴾ keep markers. Verse fragments: ﴿أَن تَعُودُواْ لِمِثْلِهِ﴾ = "that you return to the like of it"; ﴿يَعِظُكُمُ﴾ = "He admonishes you"; ﴿إِن كُنتُمْ مُّؤْمِنِينَ﴾ = "if you are believers".

Translation:

﴿That you return to the like of it﴾. Its estimated (taqdir) reading is: ﴿He admonishes you﴾ out of aversion that you return to the like of it. Then He magnified the matter and emphasized it with His words: ﴿if you are believers﴾.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on Surah 24, verse 19:

﴿Indeed, those who love that immorality should spread among those who have believed—for them is a painful punishment in this world and the Hereafter.﴾ The reference here is to the hypocrites who loved that the slander (hadith al-ifk) should be spread. Then it is general to others who have the same attribute as them. The punishment in this world is the prescribed penalty (al-hadd). As for the punishment of the Hereafter, it has been reported in a hadith that whoever is punished in this world for a sin, he will not be punished for it in the Hereafter. So the combination of the prescribed penalty with the punishment of the Hereafter in this context is problematic. It may be that the slanderer is punished in the Hereafter and the prescribed penalty does not remove the punishment of the Hereafter from him, unlike other prescribed penalties. Or this may be specific to one who slandered ʿĀʾisha, for it has been narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "Whoever commits a sin and then repents from it, his repentance is accepted, except one who engaged in the matter of ʿĀʾisha." Or it may be for one who dies persisting in sin without repenting. Or it may be for the hypocrites.
﴿the footsteps of Satan﴾ (mentioned in al-Baqarah) ﴿to indecency and wrongdoing﴾ (mentioned in al-Nahl). ﴿Zaka﴾: i.e., he became pure from sins, and his religion was made sound.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 24, verse 22:

﴿And let not those of virtue and wealth among you swear not to give [aid] to the near of kin﴾ The meaning of yata'talī is "yahlif" (swears an oath). It is derived from your saying: "ālaytu" when one swears an oath. It has also been said that its meaning is "yuqassir" (falls short, neglects), derived from your saying: "alawtu," meaning "qassartu" (I fell short). From this is ﴿they spare no effort to corrupt you﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 118]. The word fadl (virtue) here may mean either virtue in religion or virtue in wealth, namely that one has a surplus beyond what suffices him. The word saʿah (wealth/abundance) is the expansiveness of property. The verse was revealed concerning Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq (may Allah be pleased with him) when he swore that he would not spend on Mistah, after Mistah spoke in the matter of the slander (ḥadīth al-ifk). He had been spending on him because of his poverty, and because he was his relative, for he was the son of his maternal aunt. When the verse was revealed, he returned to Mistah his maintenance and kindness, and expiated for his oath. Some of them said: "This is the most hopeful verse in the Qur'an, because Allah enjoined kindness toward the slanderer." Furthermore, the wording of the verse is general in that no one should swear to abandon a righteous deed. ﴿Would you not love that Allah forgive you?﴾ That is: just as you love that Allah forgive you, so likewise forgive those who have wronged you. When it was revealed, Abū Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Indeed I love that Allah forgive me," and then he restored the maintenance to Mistah.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 24, verse 23:

﴿Those chaste, unsuspecting, believing women⁠﴾ The meaning of al-muhsanat (the chaste) here is the modest women who guard their chastity, and the meaning of al-ghafilat (the unsuspecting) is those whose hearts are sound, so it derives from being unaware of evil. ﴿They are cursed in this world and the Hereafter⁠﴾ This threat is for those who slandered ʿĀʾisha, and for that reason no repentance is mentioned in it. Ibn ʿAbbas said: every sinner's repentance is accepted if he repents, except one who plunged into the matter of ʿĀʾisha. It was also said: the threat applies to every slanderer. And the great punishment may be intended to mean the prescribed legal penalty (ḥadd) or the punishment of the Hereafter.

﴿On the Day when ... bear witness﴾. Its governing element (al-'amil) is "yuwaffihim" (He will pay them in full). He repeated "yawma'idhin" (on that day) for emphasis (tawkid). It was also said that its governing element is "'adhab" (punishment), or an implied verb.

Their due recompense, the true one (dinahum al-haqq): that is, their just reward that is owed to them. "And they will know that Allah is the Manifest Truth (al-Haqq al-Mubin)." This verse indicates that what precedes it concerns the hypocrites, because the believer already knew in this world that Allah is the Manifest Truth. Al-Mubin means the evident one, about which there is no doubt.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 24, verse 26:

﴿The wicked women are for wicked men, and the wicked men are for wicked women; and the good women are for good men, and the good men are for good women.﴾ The meaning of the verse is that wicked women are for wicked men, and good women are for good men. In this there is a refutation of the people of the slander (ahl al-ifk), because the Prophet (ﷺ) is the best of the good, so his wife is the best of the good women. It is also said that the meaning is that wicked deeds are for wicked people, and good deeds are for good people; in this too there is a refutation of the people of the slander. It is also said that the meaning is that wicked words are for wicked people, and the reference in "that" is to the people of the slander: that is, their wicked words are not uttered except by a wicked person like them. ﴿Those are cleared of what they say.﴾ The reference in "those" is to the good men and the good women, and the pronoun in "they say" refers to the wicked women and the wicked men. The intent is to clear 'Ā'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) of what she was accused of.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 24, verses 27–29:

﴿Do not enter houses other than your own until you have sought permission and greeted their occupants.﴾ This verse is a command to seek permission before entering any house other than one's own, so it covers the houses of relatives and others. A hadith has also come with the command to seek permission before entering upon one's mother, lest one see her uncovered. The meaning of ﴿tasta'nisu﴾ (seek permission) is "ta'dhinu" (ask permission). It is derived from your saying "anastu lil-shay'" (I perceived the thing) when you came to know it. So al-isti'nas (seeking permission) means to seek to know whether the people of the house wish you to enter or not. It has also been said that it is derived from "al-uns" (intimacy), the opposite of "al-wahsha" (estrangement). Ibn ʿAbbas read it as ﴿hatta tasta'dhinu﴾ (until you seek permission). Seeking permission is obligatory, whereas greeting does not reach the level of obligation. Scholars differed over which of the two should come first. It has been said that one greets first and then asks permission, saying: "Peace be upon you, may I enter?" It has also been said that permission is sought first, because the verse mentions it first. The verse does not specify the number of times permission must be sought, but a hadith has come that one should ask permission three times. This is the explanation of the verse ﴿There is no sin upon you for entering houses not inhabited, in which there is provision for you.﴾ The occasion of this verse was that when the verse of seeking permission was revealed, some people went to extremes and began to visit uninhabited places, greeting and asking permission there. So this verse permitted entering them without seeking permission. Scholars differed about what "uninhabited houses" in this verse means. It has been said that they are the inns on the roads that no one lives in, but are endowed so that every wayfarer may take shelter in them, and in this view "provision" means enjoying their use by staying and spending the night there and so on. It has also been said that they are ruined houses entered for urinating and defecating, and in this view "provision" means a person's need. It has further been said that they are the shops of the qaysariyya (covered market), and in this view "provision" means clothing, rugs and the like. But this last view is wrong, because seeking permission before entering shops is obligatory by consensus.

﴿قُلْ لِّلْمُؤْمِنِينَ يَغُضُّواْ مِنْ أَبْصَارِهِمْ وَيَحْفَظُواْ فُرُوجَهُمْ﴾ Its i'rab (grammatical analysis) is like the i'rab of ﴿يُقِيمُواْ ٱلصَّلاَةَ﴾ in Surat Ibrahim [31]. It has already been mentioned. The *min* in ﴿مِنْ أَبْصَارِهِمْ﴾ is for partitive (*tab'idh*), and the intended meaning is lowering the gaze from what is forbidden and confining it to what is permitted. It was also said that the partitive sense here means that the first glance is not sinful, but what follows it is prohibited. Al-Akhfash (al-Akhfash, a grammarian) permitted that the *min* be extra (*ziyadah*). It was also said that it is for the beginning of the extent (*ibtida' al-ghayah*), because the eye is the key to the heart. The lowering commanded is from looking at the awrah (the parts of the body that must be covered), or at women who are not lawful, or at the letters of others, and similar things that are concealed. The guarding of the private parts commanded is from unlawful intercourse. It was also said that it means covering the awrah. The more apparent view is that all of this is intended.

﴿وَقُل لِّلْمُؤْمِنَاتِ يَغْضُضْنَ مِنْ أَبْصَارِهِنَّ﴾ The woman is commanded to lower her gaze from the awrah of a man and from the awrah of a woman, by consensus (*ijma'*, the agreement of scholars). It is disputed whether she is obligated to lower her gaze from the rest of a non-mahram man's body or not, and from the rest of a woman's body or not. According to the view that it is obligatory, the verse includes it. The discussion of guarding women's private parts is the same as the guarding of men's private parts.

﴿وَلاَ يُبْدِينَ زِينَتَهُنَّ إِلاَّ مَا ظَهَرَ مِنْهَا﴾ He forbade displaying adornment in general, then excepted what appears of it, which is what cannot avoid being seen when she moves, adjusts her affairs, or the like. It was said: "except what appears of it" means the clothing. According to this, her entire body must be covered. It was also said that it means the clothing, the face, and the two hands. This is the view of Malik, because he permitted uncovering her face and hands in prayer. Abu Hanifa added the two feet.

﴿وَلْيَضْرِبْنَ بِخُمُرِهِنَّ عَلَىٰ جُيُوبِهِنَّ﴾ The *juyub* (openings of the garment at the neck and chest) are what common people call *atwaq* (collars). The reason is that women in that era wore garments with wide openings, through which their chests showed. When they covered their heads with *akhmirah* (plural of *khimar*, head-covering), they would let it hang behind their backs, so the chest, neck, and ears remained uncovered. So God commanded them to draw the *akhmirah* [plural of *khimar*] over the *juyub*, so that all of that would be covered.

﴿And marry off the unmarried among you﴾. Al-ayama is the plural of ayyim (one who has no spouse), and it means those who have no spouses, whether men or women, virgins or previously married. The address here is to the guardians and the rulers, whom God commanded to marry off the unmarried. This requires prohibiting them from preventing (adl) them from marriage. In the verse there is evidence that women do not have independent authority to contract marriage, and that guardianship (wilaya) is a condition in it, the guardianship in it. This is the position of Malik and al-Shafi'i, in contrast to Abu Hanifa.

﴿And the righteous among your male servants and your female servants﴾. This means those among the male and female slaves who are fit for marriage. Al-Zamakhshari said: "The righteous" means righteousness in religion. He said: "God singled them out for mention only to safeguard their righteousness, and the addressees here are their masters." The position of al-Shafi'i is that the master is compelled to marry off his slaves, based on this verse, in contrast to Malik. The position of Malik is that the master compels his male and female slave to marry, in contrast to al-Shafi'i.

﴿If they are poor, God will enrich them from His bounty﴾. God promised wealth to the poor who marry seeking the pleasure of God. For this reason Ibn Mas'ud said: "Seek wealth through marriage."

﴿And let those who cannot find the means to marry keep themselves chaste until Allah enriches them from His bounty.﴾ This is a command to seek chastity (al-istiʻfaf, meaning to strive to keep oneself free from what is unlawful) for the one who is unable to marry. The phrase ﴿لاَ يَجِدُونَ نِكَاحاً﴾ (lā yajidūna nikāḥan, "cannot find a marriage") means that they have no ability to marry, for whatever reason marriage is prevented. It was also said that it means they cannot find the dowry (ṣadāq) for the marriage. The first meaning is more general, while the second fits better with the words ﴿until Allah enriches them from His bounty﴾.

﴿And those who seek a deed of manumission from among those whom your right hands possess, write it for them.﴾ Here al-kitāb (الكتاب) is a verbal noun meaning kitāba (kitābah, contractual manumission): a master makes a contract with his slave for a sum of money paid in instalments (munajjam). If he pays it, he goes free; if he fails, he remains a slave. It was also said that the verse was revealed concerning Ḥuwaṭib ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā, who asked his master to write a manumission contract for him, but the master refused. Its ruling is nonetheless general: Allah commands masters to write contracts for their slaves when they ask for them. Malik and the majority (al-jumhūr) hold that this command is recommended (nadb), while the Ẓāhiriyya and others held that it is obligatory (wujūb). The clearest support for the obligatory view is the statement of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with him, to Anas ibn Mālik when his slave Sīrīn asked for a manumission contract and Anas hesitated: ʿUmar said to him, "Either you write it for him or I will beat you with the whip." Malik restricted it to recommendation because kitābah is like a sale, and just as one cannot be compelled to sell, one cannot be compelled to enter a manumission contract. Within the school there are two opinions on whether a master may be compelled to write such a contract for his slave.

﴿if you know any good in them﴾: the good (khayr) here means the ability to pay the manumission sum by any means. It was also said that it means money with which he pays his contract without asking people for their wealth, and it was said that it means righteousness in religion.

﴿and give them from the wealth of Allah which He has given you.﴾ This is a command to help the slave who is under a manumission contract (mukātab) to pay it. Scholars differed about who is addressed. It was said that it addresses all people, and it was said that it addresses the rulers. On these two views the command is recommended. It was also said that it addresses the masters of the slaves, and on this view it is recommended according to Malik, but obligatory according to al-Shāfiʿī. If the address is to all people, the meaning is that they should give them charity from their wealth; if it is to the rulers, they should give them from the zakat; if it is to the masters, they should remit part of the contract for them. It was also said that they should give them from their own wealth apart from the contract. On the view that the master remits part of the contract, scholars differed about how much is to be remitted. Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 24, verse 35:

Allah ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ [al-Shūrā: 11], so the interpretation of the verse is: Allah is the Possessor of the light of the heavens and the earth. He described Himself as light in the way you say "Zayd is generosity" when you want to emphasize that he is generous. If by *nūr* one means what is perceived by the eyes, then the meaning of "the light of the heavens and the earth" is that He created the light in them, from the sun, the moon and the stars, or that He created them and brought them from non-existence into existence, so that things became manifest through Him as things become manifest by light. In this sense, ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib read ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth﴾ with a fatḥah on the *nūn*, the *wāw* and the *rāʾ*, and a shaddah on the *wāw*, meaning: He placed light in them. If by *nūr* one means what is perceived by the hearts, then the meaning of "the light of the heavens and the earth" is He who places light in the hearts of the people of the heavens and the earth. For this reason Ibn ʿAbbās said: its meaning is "the guide of the people of the heavens and the earth."

﴿The likeness of His light is like a niche (mishkāh) in which is a lamp﴾. The *mishkāh* is a recess that is not pierced through, set in a wall, in which the lamp is very bright. It was said that the *mishkāh* is the pillar on whose top the lamp stands, but the first meaning is more correct and more well known. The meaning is that the description of the light of Allah in its clarity is like the description of a niche in which is a lamp, at the greatest level of brightness and illumination that a human can imagine. He was likened to a niche although the light of Allah is greater, because that is the furthest that people can perceive of lights, so the example was given to them by means of what they can grasp. It was said that the pronoun in *nūrih* (His light) refers to our master Muḥammad (ﷺ); it was said that it refers to the Qur'an; and it was said that it refers to the believer. These opinions are weak, because nothing preceding the verse is referred to by the pronoun. If it is said: how is it valid to say "Allah is the light of the heavens and the earth," stating that He is the light, and then to attach "light" to Him in His saying ﴿the likeness of His light﴾, when the attributed is the very same as the attributee? The answer is that this is valid with the interpretation we have already mentioned, namely: Allah is the Possessor of the light of the heavens and the earth. Or, as you say: "Zayd is generosity," and then you say: "People are sustained by his generosity."

﴿The lamp is in a glass﴾. The *miṣbāḥ* (lamp) is the wick with its fire. The meaning is that it is in a lantern of glass, because its light is brighter, since it is a transparent body. ﴿The glass is as if it were a brilliant star﴾. The glass is likened in its brightness to a shining star (*kawkab durrī*). This may have two meanings: either it means that the glass shines by the lamp within it, or it means that the glass itself is very bright because of its purity and the fineness of its substance. The second is more eloquent, since its light is combined with the light of the lamp. By *kawkab durrī* is meant one of the shining stars, such as Jupiter, Venus, Canopus and the like. It was said that it refers specifically to Venus, but there is no evidence for this restriction. Nāfiʿ read ﴿durrī﴾ with a ḍammah on the *dāl* and a shaddah on the *yāʾ*, without a *hamzah*. This reading has two possible explanations: either the star is attributed to *durr* (pearl) because of its whiteness and purity, or it is an easing (*tasḥīl*) of the *hamzah*. Ḥamzah and Abū Bakr read ﴿durriyy-un﴾ with a *hamzah* and a kasrah on the *dāl*... [text: "دُرِّيء" with hamzah and a ḍammah on the dāl], and it is derived from *al-darʾ*, meaning "repelling."

﴿It is lit from a blessed tree, an olive tree﴾. Whoever reads *yūqadu* with a *yāʾ*, or *tawaqqada* in the past tense, makes the verb refer to the lamp. Whoever reads *tūqadu* with a *tāʾ* in the present tense makes it refer to the glass. The meaning is: it is lit from the oil of a blessed tree. It was described as blessed because of its many benefits, or because it grows in the blessed land, which is al-Shām (Syria). ﴿Neither of the east nor of the west﴾. It was said: this means that it is in al-Shām, so it is neither from the eastern part of the earth nor from its western part, and the best olives are the olives of al-Shām. It was said: it is exposed, so the sun reaches it the whole day, so it is not exclusively of the east, to be called "eastern," nor exclusively of the west, to be called "western," but it is both western and eastern, because the sun turns around it from the east and the west. It was said: it is in the middle of a tree, not on the eastern side of the tree nor on its western side. It was said: it is from the tree of Paradise, and if it were in this world it would be either eastern or western. ﴿Its oil would almost glow even if no fire touched it﴾, as an exaggeration in describing its purity and excellence. ﴿Light upon light﴾ means the combination of the light of the lamp, the beauty of the glass and the goodness of the oil, and what is meant by this is the perfection of the light being likened. ﴿Allah guides to His light whom He wills﴾, that is, Allah grants success to whom He wills to reach the truth.

In houses (buyut): this means the mosques. It was also said: the houses of the people of faith, whether mosques or dwellings, though the first is more sound. The preposition "in" (fi) may be connected to what precedes it, meaning: "like a niche within houses," or "it is kindled within houses." It was also said that it is connected to what follows, "He is glorified," and the preposition was repeated afterward for emphasis. It was also said that it is connected to an omitted verb: i.e., "Glorify Him in houses which Allah has permitted to be raised" (fi buyutin adhina Allahu an turfa'a). By "permission" (idhn) is meant command. "Raising" them means building them; it was also said it means honouring them. "In the mornings and the evenings" (bil-ghuduwwi wal-asal): i.e., at dawn and at dusk. It was also said he meant the morning and afternoon prayers, and it was also said the forenoon prayer (duha) and the afternoon prayer (asr). "Men" (rijal) is the subject (fa'il) of "glorify" (yusabbihu) according to the reading with a kasra on the ba' (yusabbihu). As for the reading with a fatha on the ba' (yusabbahu), it is in the nominative by an implied verb indicated by the first one. "Neither trade nor sale diverts them from the remembrance of Allah": i.e., does not distract them. The verse was revealed concerning the people of the markets who, when they heard the call to prayer, abandoned every occupation and hastened to it. Sale (bay') is a form of trade, but he singled it out for mention for emphasis, like His saying: "Fruits, and palm trees, and pomegranates" (Al-Rahman: 68). Or he meant by trade the act of buying. "Hearts and eyes will be turned about in it" (tatagallabu fihi al-qulubu wal-absar): i.e., will be agitated from the intensity of the terror and fear. It was also said: hearts will understand and eyes will see after blindness, because the realities will be revealed at that time. The first is more sound, like His saying: "And when the eyes shall become dazed and the hearts reach the throats" (Al-Ahzab: 10). In His saying "in it the hearts turn about" there is a paronomasia (tajnis). "That Allah may reward them" (li-yajziyahumu Allahu) is connected to what precedes it, or to a verb carrying the meaning of what precedes it. "The best of what they did": its estimated sense is "a reward better than what they did." "And increase them of His bounty": i.e., an increase over the reward of their deeds. Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 24, verse 39:

﴿And as for those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a level plain﴾ When Allah mentioned the state of the believers, He followed it with two examples of the deeds of the disbelievers. The first pertains to the state of their deeds in the Hereafter, that they will not benefit them, and that their reward will vanish just as the mirage vanishes. The second pertains to the state of their deeds in this world, that they are in the utmost corruption and misguidance, like the darknesses layered one upon another. The mirage (sarab) is what is seen in the open desert, from the light of the sun at midday, until it appears as if it were water flowing over the surface of the earth. The qay'a is the plural of qa', which is the flat, level land; and it was said: it is in the sense of qa' and not a plural. ﴿Which the thirsty one thinks to be water﴾ The thirsty one (al-zam'an) is the one afflicted with thirst: that is, the thirsty person thinks the mirage is water, so he comes to it to drink it, but when he comes, what he hoped for has failed and what he supposed has come to nothing. Likewise the disbeliever thinks that his deeds will benefit him, but when the Day of Resurrection comes, they do not benefit him, so they are like the mirage. ﴿Until, when he comes to it﴾ The pronoun of the subject refers to the thirsty one, and the pronoun of the object refers to the mirage; or the pronoun of the subject refers to the disbeliever and the pronoun of the object refers to his deed. ﴿He finds it to be nothing﴾ That is, nothing from which he benefits, or nothing existent in general, since it is non-existent. It is possible that the pronoun of the subject refers to the thirsty one and the pronoun of the object to the mirage; or the pronoun of the subject refers to the disbeliever and the pronoun of the object to his deed. ﴿And he finds Allah with him﴾ The pronoun of the subject in "wajada" (he found) refers to the disbeliever, and the pronoun in "'indahu" (with him) refers to his deed; the meaning is that he finds Allah with it, by way of recompense, or he finds the guardians of Allah (zabaniyya).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 24, verses 40–44:

﴿Or like darknesses﴾. This is the second example, and it is coordinated with His words ﴿like a mirage﴾. What is compared to the darknesses is the deeds of the disbelievers. That is, they are in misguidance and bewilderment like darknesses piled upon one another: the darkness of the sea, beneath the waves, beneath the clouds. ﴿In a deep sea﴾. The word "lujjiy" is derived from "lujj", which means the greatest body of water. Some scholars held that the parts of this example correspond to the parts of what it illustrates: the darknesses are the deeds of the disbeliever, the deep sea is his breast, the waves are his ignorance, and the clouds are the covering over his heart. Others held that it is an illustration as a whole, without point-by-point correspondence. Describing these darknesses with these attributes is an intensification, just as the description of the light mentioned before it is an intensification. ﴿When he extends his hand, he can hardly see it﴾. The meaning is an intensification in describing the darkness. The pronoun in "akhraja" (extended) and what follows it refers to the man who has fallen into the described darknesses. The scholars differed on the interpretation of the statement. It was said: the meaning is that when he extends his hand, he does not come close to seeing it, so seeing it and approaching seeing it are both negated. It was also said: rather, he sees it after difficulty and hardship, because "kāda" (he almost did), when negated, implies affirmation, and when affirmed, implies negation. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: this applies only when the negative particle enters upon the verb that follows it. But when the negative particle enters upon "kāda" itself, as in the saying "lam yakad" (he did not almost), it admits both negation and affirmation.

﴿And whoever Allah does not give light, for him there is no light﴾. That is, whoever Allah does not guide is not guided. So "light" is a metaphor for guidance and faith in this world. It was also said that He intended the Hereafter, meaning whoever Allah does not show mercy to has no mercy. The first interpretation fits better with what precedes it. ﴿Do you not see that to Allah glorify whoever is in the heavens and the earth, and the birds in flight with wings spread?﴾. "Seeing" here means knowing, and "tasbīḥ" (glorification) means declaring Allah transcendent and magnifying Him. This applies to rational beings through speech. As for the glorification of birds and other things that do not reason, the majority of scholars (al-jumhūr) said that it is literal, and it is not far-fetched that Allah inspires them with glorification, just as He inspires them with subtle matters that rational beings cannot discover. It was said that their glorification is the manifestation of wisdom in them. ﴿Spreading their wings﴾: arranging their wings in the air. ﴿He knows well each one's prayer and glorification﴾. The pronoun in "ʿalima" (He knows) refers to Allah, or it refers to each (of the creatures). The pronoun in "ṣalātahu wa-tasbīḥahu" (his prayer and his glorification) refers to each one. ﴿Drives﴾ means drives onward. "Izjāʾ" is used only for driving a heavy thing, such as clouds. ﴿Piled up﴾: its parts are densely compacted, one upon another. ﴿The rain﴾ (al-wadq). ﴿From within it﴾: from between it. "Khilāl" is the plural of "khalal", like "jabal" and "jibāl" (mountain and mountains). ﴿And He sends down from the sky mountains [of clouds] wherein is hail﴾. It was said that the mountains here are literal, and that Allah placed in the sky mountains of hail. It was also said that it is figurative, like your saying "there are mountains of wealth or knowledge with so-and-so", meaning they are as abundant as mountains. The "min" in His words ﴿from the sky﴾ indicates the starting point, and so does the "min" in ﴿mountains﴾. The latter is a substitute for the former. It may be partitive, in which case it is the object of "yunazzilu" (He sends down). The "min" in ﴿of hail﴾ is either explanatory of the genus or partitive, in which case it is the object of "yunazzilu". Al-Akhfash said that it is superfluous, but this is weak. His words ﴿wherein﴾ are a description of the mountains, and the pronoun refers to the sky. ﴿The brilliance of its lightning﴾. "Sanā" with a short vowel means light, and with a long vowel means glory and nobility. ﴿Allah alternates the night and the day﴾: that is, He brings this after that.

Some scholars held that the parts of this example correspond to the parts of what it illustrates: the darknesses are the deeds of the disbeliever, the deep sea is his breast, the waves are his ignorance, and the clouds are the covering over his heart. Others held that it is an illustration as a whole, without point-by-point correspondence. Describing these darknesses with these attributes is an intensification, just as the description of the light mentioned before it is an intensification. ﴿When he extends his hand, he can hardly see it﴾. The meaning is an intensification in describing the darkness. The pronoun in "akhraja" (extended) and what follows it refers to the man who has fallen into the described darknesses. The scholars differed on the interpretation of the statement. It was said: the meaning is that when he extends his hand, he does not come close to seeing it, so seeing it and approaching seeing it are both negated. It was also said: rather, he sees it after difficulty and hardship, because "kāda" (he almost did), when negated, implies affirmation, and when affirmed, implies negation. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: this applies only when the negative particle enters upon the verb that follows it. But when the negative particle enters upon "kāda" itself, as in the saying "lam yakad" (he did not almost), it admits both negation and affirmation.

﴿And whoever Allah does not give light, for him there is no light﴾. That is, whoever Allah does not guide is not guided. So "light" is a metaphor for guidance and faith in this world. It was also said that He intended the Hereafter, meaning whoever Allah does not show mercy to has no mercy. The first interpretation fits better with what precedes it. ﴿Do you not see that to Allah glorify whoever is in the heavens and the earth, and the birds in flight with wings spread?﴾. "Seeing" here means knowing, and "tasbīḥ" (glorification) means declaring Allah transcendent and magnifying Him. This applies to rational beings through speech. As for the glorification of birds and other things that do not reason, the majority of scholars (al-jumhūr) said that it is literal, and it is not far-fetched that Allah inspires them with glorification, just as He inspires them with subtle matters that rational beings cannot discover. It was said that their glorification is the manifestation of wisdom in them. ﴿Spreading their wings﴾: arranging their wings in the air. ﴿He knows well each one's prayer and glorification﴾. The pronoun in "ʿalima" (He knows) refers to Allah, or it refers to each (of the creatures). The pronoun in "ṣalātahu wa-tasbīḥahu" (his prayer and his glorification) refers to each one. ﴿Drives﴾ means drives onward. "Izjāʾ" is used only for driving a heavy thing, such as clouds. ﴿Piled up﴾: its parts are densely compacted, one upon another. ﴿The rain﴾ (al-wadq). ﴿From within it﴾: from between it. "Khilāl" is the plural of "khalal", like "jabal" and "jibāl" (mountain and mountains). ﴿And He sends down from the sky mountains [of clouds] wherein is hail﴾. It was said that the mountains here are literal, and that Allah placed in the sky mountains of hail. It was also said that it is figurative, like your saying "there are mountains of wealth or knowledge with so-and-so", meaning they are as abundant as mountains. The "min" in His words ﴿from the sky﴾ indicates the starting point, and so does the "min" in ﴿mountains﴾. The latter is a substitute for the former. It may be partitive, in which case it is the object of "yunazzilu" (He sends down). The "min" in ﴿of hail﴾ is either explanatory of the genus or partitive, in which case it is the object of "yunazzilu". Al-Akhfash said that it is superfluous, but this is weak. His words ﴿wherein﴾ are a description of the mountains, and the pronoun refers to the sky. ﴿The brilliance of its lightning﴾. "Sanā" with a short vowel means light, and with a long vowel means glory and nobility. ﴿Allah alternates the night and the day﴾: that is, He brings this after that.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 24, verse 45:

﴿Allah created every creature﴾ (dābba), meaning the children of Adam, the livestock and the birds, because all of these move (yadibb) along the ground. ﴿from water﴾, meaning the seminal fluid (al-maniyy). It is also said: it is the water that is in the clay from which Adam and others were created. ﴿of them some walk on their bellies﴾ like snakes and fish.

﴿They say, "We believe"﴾ and the rest of the verse: It was revealed concerning the hypocrites. The occasion of its revelation was that a man among the hypocrites had a dispute with a Jew. The Jew invited him to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for judgment, but he turned away from him and invited him instead to Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 24, verse 49:

﴿مُذْعِنِينَ﴾ meaning: submissive and compliant, eager to obtain their rights.

Translation:

﴿Is there a disease in their hearts?﴾ This is a tawqif (a question meant as a rebuke), and the same applies to what follows. ﴿Lest He should wrong them﴾: its meaning is "lest He should act unjustly," and al-hayf is inclination (al-mayl). He attributed it to Allah, because the Messenger only judges by the command and law of Allah.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 24, verse 51:

﴿Indeed, the saying of the believers﴾ [the rest of the verse]. Its meaning: the obligation is only that the believers say, "We hear and we obey," when they are called to Allah and His Messenger; and He made the call to Allah, as such, to be a call to His law.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 24, verse 52:

﴿And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger﴾ — the verse. Ibn ʿAbbas said: its meaning is: whoever obeys Allah in His obligatory duties and His Messenger in his sunnah, ﴿and fears Allah﴾ regarding his past sins, ﴿and is mindful of Him﴾ regarding what lies ahead. Some kings asked about a sufficient and comprehensive verse, so this verse was mentioned to him. One of the patricians (baṭāriqa) of the Romans heard it and embraced Islam, and said that it combined everything in the Torah and the Gospel.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 24, verses 53–54:

﴿And they swore﴾, i.e., they took oaths, the pronoun referring to the hypocrites, ﴿by their most emphatic oaths﴾, i.e., they went to the utmost in swearing and confirmed them, ﴿that they would surely go forth﴾, meaning to the military campaign. ﴿Say: Do not swear﴾. He forbade false oaths, because He knew that they swear to falsehood. ﴿Obedience is known﴾: it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate (khabar) is omitted, meaning: obedience that is known is more fitting and more appropriate for you; or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: what is required of you is known obedience, about which there is no doubt. ﴿On him is what he has been charged with﴾, meaning the conveying of the message, ﴿and on you is what you have been charged with﴾, meaning hearing and obeying and following the Sharia.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 24, verses 53–54:

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 24, verse 55:

﴿Surely He will make them successors in the earth﴾ — a promise whose truth has become manifest through the conquest of the eastern and western regions of the earth for this Ummah. It has also been said that the intended meaning of the verse is the caliphate of Abu Bakr, ʿUthman and ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with them, based on the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "The caliphate after me will be thirty years," and the thirty years ended with the end of the caliphate of ʿAli. If it is said: where is the oath to which the words ﴿He will surely make them successors﴾ serve as the answer? The answer is that it is omitted, its estimated form being: "Allah promised them and swore," or the promise is treated as equivalent to an oath because of its certainty.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 24, verse 58:

﴿Let those whom your right hands possess ask your permission﴾ It has been said that what is meant by "those whom your right hands possess" is men specifically, and it has been said women specifically, because men ask permission at every time. It has also been said men and women. ﴿And those who have not yet reached puberty﴾ meaning children who have not reached puberty. ﴿Three times﴾ is in the accusative as an adverb of time, because they were commanded to ask permission at three occasions. The meaning of the verse, then, is that God commanded the slaves and the children to ask permission at three times: before the dawn prayer, at midday when people lay down their clothes (al-qa'ila), and after the last night prayer (al-'isha'), because at these times people are for the most part undressed for sleep. This is a muhkam verse (a clear, non-abrogated verse). Ibn 'Abbas said: "People have abandoned acting upon it." Some scholars understood it as recommended (nadb).

﴿You put off your clothes﴾ meaning you undress. ﴿At noon﴾ meaning the middle of the day. ﴿Three times of nakedness﴾ "'awrat" is the plural of "'awra," from exposure, as in His saying: ﴿Our houses are exposed ('awra)﴾ [al-Ahzab: 13]. Whoever reads "thalath" in the nominative is saying it is the predicate of an implied subject, its estimate being: these times are three occasions of nakedness for you, i.e., you are exposed in them. Whoever reads it in the accusative makes it a substitute (badal) for "three times."

﴿There is no sin upon you or upon them beyond these﴾ The feminine pronoun refers to the preceding times, i.e., there is no sin upon you, nor upon the slaves and children, in omitting to ask permission outside these three occasions. ﴿They move about among you﴾ its estimate: the slaves and children move about among you; therefore they are commanded to ask permission at every time. ﴿Some of you upon others﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "they move about among you," i.e., some of you go about upon others. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is the subject (mubtada') meaning some of you go about upon others, or it is the agent (fa'il) of an implied verb.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 24, verse 59:

﴿And when the children among you reach puberty, let them ask permission﴾ Since, in the preceding verse, He commanded children to seek permission at three times, and permitted them to enter without permission at other times, He here commands them to seek permission at all times once they have reached puberty and joined the men.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 24, verse 60:

﴿And the women who are past child-bearing (al-qawa'id min al-nisa')﴾ is the plural of qā'id, and it refers to an old woman. It has been said: she is the one who has ceased to bear children. It has also been said: she is the one who has ceased to display herself (al-tabarruj).

﴿there is no blame upon them for laying aside their outer garments﴾. Allah permitted this category of elderly women what He did not permit to others of laying aside garments. Ibn Mas'ud said: what is permitted to them is laying aside the jilbab that is worn over the khimar and the rida'. Some of them said: this applies only in her own home, where her close relatives (dhu mahaarimiha) see her.

﴿without intending a display of adornment (ghayra mutabarrijatin bi-zinah)﴾. Allah only permitted them to lay aside their garments on the condition that they do not intend to show adornment. Tabarruj means to display oneself (al-zuhur).

﴿but to refrain is better for them (wa-an yasta'fifna khayrun lahunna)﴾. The meaning is that abstaining from laying aside the aforementioned garments is better for them than laying them aside, and it is preferable for them to adhere to what young women are required to adhere to of covering.

The verse "There is no blame upon the blind..." (﴿لَّيْسَ عَلَى ٱلأَعْمَىٰ حَرَجٌ﴾) and what follows. Scholars differ about the matter in which the blame is lifted from the blind, the lame, and the sick in this verse. It has been said that it concerns the military campaign (ghazw), meaning there is no blame on them for staying behind from it. On this view, the phrase ﴿وَلاَ عَلَىٰ أَنفُسِكُمْ﴾ ("nor upon yourselves") is separate from what precedes it, as if He said: there is no blame on these three for abstaining from the campaign, and no blame on you regarding eating.

It has also been said that the whole verse concerns eating. Those who hold this differ. Some said: the people of these excuses used to avoid eating with others, lest people find them repulsive, so the verse was revealed permitting them to eat with people. Others said: when the people set out for the campaign, they left the people of these excuses at home, and the people used to avoid eating the property of the absent, so the verse was revealed concerning that. Others said: people used to avoid eating with them out of disgust, so the verse was revealed. This last view is weak, because the lifting of blame applies to the people of excuses and not to others.

It has further been said that the lifting of blame from these three extends to everything their excuses prevent them from, such as jihad and other things.

﴿وَلاَ عَلَىٰ أَنفُسِكُمْ أَن تَأْكُلُواْ مِن بُيُوتِكُمْ﴾ ("nor upon yourselves that you eat from your houses"): God, exalted is He, permitted a person to eat in the houses mentioned in the verse. He began with the house of the man himself, then mentioned the relatives in their order, and did not mention the son, because he is included in His words ﴿مِن بُيُوتِكُمْ﴾ ("from your houses"), since the son's house is his father's house, based on the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "You and your wealth belong to your father."

Scholars differed about the eating from the houses of relatives mentioned in this verse. A group held that it has been abrogated (mansukh, "abrogated") and that it is not permitted to eat from anyone's house except with his permission. The abrogating text (nasikh) is God's words: ﴿وَلاَ تَأْكُلُوۤاْ أَمْوَالَكُمْ بَيْنَكُمْ بِٱلْبَاطِلِ﴾ ("Do not consume one another's wealth unjustly") (Al-Baqarah 2:188; An-Nisa 4:29), and the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "The property of a Muslim man is not lawful except with his own good pleasure." Others said the verse is unabrogated (muhkam, "definitive, not abrogated"), and its meaning is the permissibility of eating from the houses of relatives when they give permission, while others said it is permitted with or without permission.

﴿أَوْ مَا مَلَكْتُمْ مَّفَاتِحهُ﴾ ("or from what you hold the keys to"): meaning the agents, the hired workers, and the slaves who hold the keys to the storehouses of their masters' wealth; He permitted them to eat from it. It has been said the meaning is what a person owns of the keys to his own self, but this view is weak.

﴿أَوْ صَدِيقِكُمْ﴾ ("or your friend"): the word ṣadīq ("friend") applies to one and to many, like ʿadūw ("enemy"). Here it is used in the plural to fit the plurals mentioned before it, in His words ﴿آبَآئِكُمْ﴾ ("your fathers") and ﴿أُمَّهَاتِكُمْ﴾ ("your mothers"), and so on. God linked the friend with the relatives because of the closeness of his affection. Ibn Abbas said: the friend is more emphatic than the relative.

﴿لَيْسَ عَلَيْكُمْ جُنَاحٌ أَن تَأْكُلُواْ جَمِيعاً أَوْ أَشْتَاتاً﴾ ("There is no blame upon you to eat together or separately"): a permission to eat both in company and alone, because some Arabs never ate alone, out of fear of stinginess, so God permitted them this.

﴿فَإِذَا دَخَلْتُمْ بُيُوتاً فَسَلِّمُواْ عَلَىٰ أَنفُسِكُمْ﴾ ("When you enter houses, greet one another"): that is, when you enter inhabited houses, greet the people in them. He said ﴿عَلَىٰ أَنفُسِكُمْ﴾ ("upon yourselves") to mean "upon your own kind," like His words ﴿وَلاَ تَلْمِزُوۤاْ أَنفُسَكُمْ﴾ ("nor defame one another") (Al-Hujurat 49:11). It has been said that the meaning is: when you enter empty houses, greet yourselves, by a man saying: "Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of God." It has also been said that by "houses" is meant mosques, and the command is to greet those in them; if there is no one in them, one greets the Prophet (ﷺ), the angels, and the righteous servants of God.

"And when they are with him on a matter of common concern" — the verse: al-amr al-jami' (a matter that gathers the people) is that which brings people together for consultation about it or for cooperating on it. This verse was revealed at the time of the digging of the trench (al-khandaq) in Madinah, for some of the believers used to ask permission to leave for a necessity, while the hypocrites (al-munafiqun) would depart without asking permission ﴿for some of their affairs﴾, meaning for some of their needs.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 24, verse 63:

﴿Do not make the call of the Messenger among yourselves like the call of some of you to others.﴾ Regarding its meaning there are three opinions. The first: the "call" here refers to the Prophet's ﷺ calling them to gather with him for a matter requiring assembly, or for fighting, or the like. The meaning is that your response to him when he calls you is obligatory, unlike when one of you calls another. This is like His saying, ﴿Respond to Allah and to the Messenger when he calls you﴾ [al-Anfal: 24]. What strengthens this view is its connection to what precedes it concerning seeking permission and a gathering matter. The second opinion: the meaning is, do not call the Messenger, peace be upon him, by his name as some of you call others by their names; rather say, "O Messenger of Allah" or "O Prophet of Allah," as a mark of honor for him and calling him by his most noble titles. It was also said: the meaning is, do not consider the Messenger's supplication against you to be like one person's supplication against another; that is, his supplication against you is answered, so beware of it. The wording of the verse is distant from this meaning, though the meaning is sound. ﴿Allah already knows those of you who slip away, sheltering themselves﴾ — those who depart from digging the trench. Al-liwadh means evasion, turning away, and opposition. It was also said it means departing secretly. ﴿So let those who oppose his command beware﴾ — the pronoun refers to Allah and His Messenger ﷺ. Scholars differed about the word "ʿan" (from) here. It was said it is superfluous (zāʾida), but this is weak. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: its meaning is that their opposition occurs after his command, as you say, "the rain came from a wind" (kāna al-maṭar ʿan rīḥ). Al-Zamakhshari said: it is said "khalafahu ilā al-amr" when one goes to it without him, and "khalafahu ʿan al-amr" when one turns people away from it. So the meaning of "yukhalifūna ʿan amrihi" is that they turn people away from it, and the object is omitted because the point is mentioning the one who opposes. ﴿A trial will befall them or a painful punishment will strike them﴾ — the trial in this world by calamities, or by disgrace or killing, or the punishment in the Hereafter.

Qad (indeed) is used here for emphasis, and the statement carries a sense of warning. It was said that its meaning is minimization, in the manner of mockery. The address is to all of creation, or to the hypocrites specifically. "And the Day they are returned to Him" means the hypocrites. The governing element of the adverbial phrase is "among them."

Note: I have translated the passage as it stands. The Qur'anic quotations are rendered as: ﴿Indeed, He knows what you are upon﴾ and ﴿And the Day they are returned to Him﴾.
